title: Book IV: Three Love Problems — Chapter XXXIX
paragraphs:
“If, as I have, you also doe,
Vertue attired in woman see,
And dare love that, and say so too,
And forget the He and She;

And if this love, though placed so,
From prophane men you hide,
Which will no faith on this bestow,
Or, if they doe, deride:

Then you have done a braver thing
Than all the Worthies did,
And a braver thence will spring,
Which is, to keep that hid.”
—DR. DONNE.

Sir James Chettam was not inventive, but his growing wish to bring pressure on Brooke, combined with his lasting faith in Dorothea’s influence, finally produced a small scheme. He would use Celia’s feeling unwell as a reason to fetch Dorothea alone to the Hall. On the way, after explaining the whole situation concerning her uncle’s management of his estate, he would leave her at the Grange with the carriage.
And so, one afternoon near four, as Mr. Brooke and Ladislaw sat in the library, the door opened and Mrs. Casaubon was announced.

A moment earlier Will had been sunk in boredom. Obliged to help Mr. Brooke arrange “documents” on hanging sheep-stealers, he was demonstrating the mind’s ability to ride several horses at once: inwardly he was planning to find lodgings in Middlemarch and end his continual residence at the Grange. Through these more settled thoughts flickered the amusing vision of an epic about sheep-stealing, written with Homer’s wealth of detail. At the announcement of Mrs. Casaubon he sprang up as though shocked by electricity, his fingertips tingling. Anyone watching would have noticed a change in his color, in the set of his face, in the brightness of his eyes, as if every particle of his body had relayed news of a magical touch. And it had. Magic that works is nature surpassing itself. Who can measure the delicacy of those impressions that carry the character of a soul as well as a body? They make a man’s passion for one woman differ from his passion for another as delight in morning light over a valley, river and white mountain summit differs from delight among Chinese lanterns and glass panels. Will, moreover, was exceptionally responsive. A skilfully drawn violin bow nearby could change the whole appearance of the world for him in a stroke; his outlook shifted as readily as his mood. Dorothea’s arrival brought the freshness of morning.
“Well, my dear, what a pleasure,” said Mr. Brooke, coming forward to kiss her. “Left Casaubon with his books, I suppose? Quite right. We mustn’t let you grow too learned for a woman, you know.”

“No danger of that, uncle,” Dorothea said. She turned and shook Will’s hand with frank good humor, offering no other greeting before continuing her answer to her uncle. “I learn very slowly. When I mean to concentrate on books, my thoughts often run off to play. Becoming learned isn’t nearly as easy as planning cottages.”
She sat beside her uncle, opposite Will, plainly absorbed in something that almost drove him from her attention. He felt absurdly disappointed, as though he had supposed she had come on his account.

“Yes, my dear, drawing plans was quite a hobby of yours. Still, it was good to interrupt it for a while. Hobbies can run away with us, you know; we mustn’t allow that. We must hold the reins. I’ve never let anything run away with me; I’ve always pulled up. That’s what I tell Ladislaw. He’s like me, you know: likes to look into everything. We’re working on capital punishment. Ladislaw and I will accomplish a great deal together.”

“Yes,” said Dorothea with her usual directness. “Sir James tells me he hopes to see a great improvement in the way your estate is managed soon. You’re considering a valuation of the farms, repairs and better cottages, so that Tipton will become quite a different place. Oh, how wonderful!” She clasped her hands, recovering the eager, childlike manner marriage had subdued. “If I still lived here, I’d start riding again so I could go round with you and see it all! And Sir James says you’re going to employ Mr. Garth, who admired my cottages.”
“Chettam is a little premature, my dear,” said Mr. Brooke, coloring faintly. “Rather premature, you know. I never said I would do anything of the sort. Nor did I say I wouldn’t, you understand.”

“He’s simply sure you will,” Dorothea answered, her voice as clear and confident as a young chorister singing a creed, “because you intend to enter Parliament as someone concerned with improving people’s lives. And the condition of the land and the laborers must be among the first things improved. Think of Kit Downes, uncle, with his wife and seven children in a house whose only rooms are a sitting room and a bedroom scarcely bigger than this table! And the poor Dagleys in that collapsing farmhouse, living in the back kitchen and leaving the rest to the rats! That’s one reason I disliked the pictures here, dear uncle—the thing you thought so stupid of me. I used to return from the village carrying all its dirt and ugly harshness like a pain inside me. Then those simpering pictures in the drawing room seemed a wicked effort to enjoy something false while we ignored how hard reality was for our neighbors outside these walls. I don’t think we have any right to advocate wider improvements until we’ve tried to remedy the wrongs within our own reach.”

As she spoke, Dorothea grew more emotional, forgetting everything except the relief of letting her feelings pour out unchecked. That had once been a familiar experience, but since her marriage it had almost disappeared into a constant struggle between her energy and her fear. For the moment, Will’s admiration carried a chilling sense of distance. A man is seldom ashamed to feel that discovering greatness in a woman makes him love her less: nature, after all, meant greatness for men. Yet nature has sometimes made unfortunate mistakes in carrying out that intention. Good Mr. Brooke was a case in point. Under his niece’s eloquence, his masculine consciousness had become rather inarticulate. For a while the only expression he could find was to stand up, adjust his eyeglass and finger the papers before him. At last he spoke—

“There’s something in what you say, my dear, something in it—but not everything, eh, Ladislaw? You and I don’t care to hear our pictures and statues criticized. Young ladies are rather fervent, you know—a little one-sided, my dear. Art, poetry and so forth raise a nation—_emollit mores_—you understand some Latin now. But—eh? What is it?”
These last questions were directed to the footman, who had entered to report that the gamekeeper had caught one of Dagley’s boys holding a young hare he had just killed.
“I’m coming, I’m coming. I’ll let him off lightly, you know,” Mr. Brooke told Dorothea aside, shuffling away in quite a cheerful mood.
“I hope you see how right these changes are—the ones I, that is, Sir James wants,” Dorothea said to Will as soon as her uncle had left.

“I do, after hearing you speak. I won’t forget what you’ve said. But could you turn your thoughts to something else just now? I may not get another chance to tell you what has happened,” Will said. He rose impatiently and gripped the back of his chair with both hands.

“Please tell me,” Dorothea said anxiously. She too stood, going to the open window where Monk was peering in, panting and wagging his tail. Leaning against the window frame, she rested a hand on his head. For although, as we know, she disliked pets that had to be carried or were always underfoot, she respected dogs’ feelings and was invariably polite when she had to refuse their attentions.
Will followed her with his eyes alone. “I assume you know Mr. Casaubon has forbidden me to visit his house.”

“No, I didn’t,” Dorothea said after a pause, visibly distressed. “I’m very, very sorry,” she added sadly. She was remembering something Will knew nothing about: her conversation with her husband in the dark. Once more she despaired of influencing Mr. Casaubon’s conduct. But the particular look of her grief persuaded Will that it was not entirely for him personally, and that she had never imagined herself to be the cause of Mr. Casaubon’s dislike and jealousy. He felt a strange mixture of pleasure and frustration. He delighted in the thought that he could live, cherished and unsuspected, in the pure home of her mind, without limits on her kindness. Yet it vexed him that he mattered too little to her, that he was not dangerous enough: her unhesitating benevolence did nothing for his vanity. Still, his fear of any change in Dorothea outweighed his dissatisfaction, and when he spoke again he adopted a merely explanatory tone.

“Mr. Casaubon gives as his reason his disapproval of my taking a job here which he thinks beneath my standing as his cousin. I’ve told him I can’t yield on that point. It’s rather hard to expect my whole life to be obstructed by prejudices I consider ridiculous. Gratitude can be stretched until it becomes no better than a slave’s brand, stamped on us before we were old enough to understand it. I wouldn’t have accepted the position unless I intended to make it useful and honorable. I owe no other kind of consideration to the family’s dignity.”
Dorothea felt miserable. She believed her husband entirely wrong, for reasons beyond those Will had mentioned.
“Since you and Mr. Casaubon disagree, we had better not discuss it,” she said, with an unusual tremor in her voice. “You mean to stay?” She looked out over the lawn in sorrowful thought.
“Yes. But now I’ll scarcely ever see you,” Will said, his complaint sounding almost like a boy’s.
“No,” Dorothea replied, looking straight at him. “Scarcely ever. But I’ll hear about you. I’ll know what you’re doing for my uncle.”
“I’ll hear almost nothing about you,” said Will. “There’ll be no one to tell me.”
“Oh, my life is very simple,” said Dorothea. An exquisite smile curved her lips and lit up her sadness. “I’m always at Lowick.”
“What a dreadful prison,” Will exclaimed impulsively.
“No, you mustn’t think that,” said Dorothea. “I don’t long for anything.”

He said nothing, but some change in his face prompted her to continue. “For myself, I mean. Except that I wish I didn’t have so much more than my share while doing nothing for others. But I have a belief of my own that comforts me.”
“What belief?” asked Will, feeling rather jealous of it.

“That when we desire perfect goodness, even without quite knowing what it is, and without being able to do all we wish, we become part of the divine power resisting evil. We spread the edges of the light and reduce the ground on which darkness can fight.”
“That’s a beautiful form of mysticism—it’s a—”

“Please don’t give it a name,” said Dorothea, holding out her hands in appeal. “You’ll call it Persian, or attach some other place to it. It’s my life. I’ve discovered it for myself and can’t give it up. I’ve been discovering my religion ever since I was a little girl. I used to pray so much; now I hardly pray at all. I try not to want things just for myself, because they may not be good for other people, and I already have too much. I only told you so you would really understand how I spend my days at Lowick.”
“God bless you for telling me!” Will said fervently, a little surprised at himself. They looked at one another like two affectionate children sharing secrets about birds.
“What is your religion?” Dorothea asked. “I don’t mean what you know about religion. I mean the belief that gives you the most help.”
“To love goodness and beauty wherever I find them,” said Will. “But I’m rebellious. I don’t feel obliged, as you do, to submit to things I dislike.”
“But if what you like is good, it amounts to the same thing,” Dorothea said, smiling.
“Now you’re being subtle,” Will replied.

“Yes, Mr. Casaubon often tells me I’m too subtle. I never feel as though I am,” said Dorothea playfully. “But how long uncle is taking! I must find him. I really must get on to the Hall; Celia is waiting for me.”

Will offered to fetch Mr. Brooke. He soon appeared and said he would join Dorothea in the carriage as far as Dagley’s, where he wanted to speak about the young offender caught with the hare. During the drive Dorothea returned to the estate, but this time Mr. Brooke was prepared and took control of the conversation.

“Now, Chettam,” he answered, “finds fault with me, my dear. But I wouldn’t preserve game at all if it weren’t for him, and he can’t claim that expense benefits the tenants. It goes rather against my feelings. Poaching, for instance, if you examine it—I’ve often thought of taking up the subject. Not long ago Flavell, the Methodist preacher, was brought before us for knocking down a hare that crossed his path when he was out walking with his wife. Very quick he was; struck it on the neck.”
“I think that was very cruel,” Dorothea said.

“Well, I admit it seemed rather bad to me, coming from a Methodist preacher, you know. And Johnson said, ‘You can see what a hypo_crite_ he is.’ Really, Flavell hardly looked like ‘the highest style of man’—someone’s description of the Christian. Young, the poet Young, I think. You know Young? Well, there was Flavell in his shabby black gaiters, arguing that the Lord had sent him and his wife a good dinner and he had a right to knock it down, though he wasn’t a mighty hunter before the Lord like Nimrod. I assure you, it was quite comic. Fielding could have done something with it, or Scott—Scott might have worked it up. But when I really thought about it, I couldn’t help being pleased that the fellow should have a bit of hare to say grace over. It’s all prejudice—prejudice backed by the law, you know—about his stick and gaiters and so on. Still, reasoning about these things won’t do; the law’s the law. But I quieted Johnson and hushed it up. I suspect Chettam might have treated him more severely, yet he attacks me as if I were the hardest man in the county. Here we are at Dagley’s.”

Mr. Brooke stepped down at a gate into the farmyard, and Dorothea drove on. Things can look astonishingly uglier as soon as we suspect someone blames us for them. Even our own reflection may change after we hear a frank comment on its less attractive features. Conversely, it is remarkable how easily conscience tolerates our trespasses against people who never complain, or have no one to complain for them. Dagley’s farm had never looked so bleak to Mr. Brooke as it did today, with his mind smarting from the “Trumpet’s” criticisms and Sir James’s repetition of them.

Of course, an observer under that softening spell of art which makes other people’s hardships picturesque might have been delighted by this farmstead, Freeman’s End. Dormer windows broke the old house’s dark red roof; ivy choked two chimneys; bundles of sticks blocked the wide porch. Half the windows were shut behind gray, worm-eaten shutters, around which jasmine branches tangled luxuriantly. The crumbling garden wall, with hollyhocks peering over it, offered a perfect study in mingled, muted colors. An elderly goat lay against the open back-kitchen door, no doubt kept for some interesting superstitious reason. The cowshed’s mossy thatch; the broken gray barn doors; the impoverished laborers in ragged breeches, almost finished unloading a wagon of grain for early threshing; the meagre dairy herd being tied up for milking, leaving half the shed brown and empty; even the pigs and white ducks wandering the neglected, uneven yard as if depressed by the thinness of the scraps they lived on—all this, under the gentle light of a sky marbled with high clouds, would have made the sort of picture we have all stopped to admire as “a charming little scene.” It would touch feelings quite different from those aroused by the agricultural depression and the miserable shortage of farming capital so often discussed in that period’s newspapers. But those troublesome connections were very much in Mr. Brooke’s mind just now, and spoiled the view. Mr. Dagley himself supplied a figure in the landscape, carrying a pitchfork and wearing his milking hat, a very old beaver hat flattened at the front. His coat and breeches were his best. He would not have worn them on a working day if he had not been to market and returned unusually late after treating himself to dinner at the Blue Bull’s communal table. Tomorrow he might wonder what had tempted him into such extravagance. Before dinner, though, something about the state of the country, the brief pause in harvesting before cutting the Far Dips, the stories about the new King and the handbills covering the walls had seemed to justify a little recklessness. Middlemarch took it as an unquestionable rule that good meat deserved good drink. Dagley understood this to mean plenty of ale with the meal, followed generously by rum and water. Those drinks contained at least this much truth: they could not lie enough to make poor Dagley cheerful. They merely loosened the tongue of his discontent. He had also swallowed too much muddled political talk, a stimulant dangerously unsettling to his farmer’s conservatism—the belief that everything as it stood was bad, and any change would probably make it worse. Flushed, his eyes fixed in an unmistakably quarrelsome stare, he stood gripping his pitchfork as his landlord approached with an easy shuffle, one hand in his trouser pocket, the other swinging a slender walking stick.
“Dagley, my good man,” Mr. Brooke began, aware of his own intention to be very kindly about the boy.

“Oh, so I’m a good man, am I? Thank you, sir, thank you,” Dagley replied with a loud, snarling sarcasm. Fag the sheepdog stirred and pricked up his ears, but on seeing Monk enter after lingering outside the yard, he sat down again to watch. “Glad to hear I’m such a good man.”

Mr. Brooke remembered that it was market day and supposed his worthy tenant had been dining. Still, he saw no reason not to proceed, provided he took the precaution of repeating his instructions to Mrs. Dagley.

“Your young Jacob was caught killing a young hare, Dagley. I’ve told Johnson to shut him in the empty stable for an hour or two, just to frighten him, you understand. He’ll be brought home before dark. You’ll keep an eye on him and tell him off, won’t you?”
“No, I won’t. I’ll be damned if I thrash my boy to please you or anyone else—not if you were twenty landlords instead of one, and a bad one at that.”

Dagley’s loud words brought his wife to the back-kitchen door, the house’s only entrance in use, which always stood open except in bad weather. “Well, well, I’ll speak to your wife. I didn’t mean a beating, you know,” Mr. Brooke said soothingly, and turned towards the house. But a gentleman walking away only strengthened Dagley’s determination to have his say. He followed immediately, with Fag slouching at his heels and sullenly dodging the small, probably well-meant approaches Monk was making.

“How are you, Mrs. Dagley?” Mr. Brooke asked rather hastily. “I’ve come about your boy. I don’t want you to beat him with a stick, you understand.” This time he took care to make himself perfectly clear.

Overworked Mrs. Dagley was a thin, worn woman whose life had been emptied of pleasure so completely that she had not even Sunday clothes to give her satisfaction in dressing for church. Since her husband’s return they had already quarreled, and now she felt low and expected the worst. He answered before she could.

“No, and he won’t get a beating, whether you want it or not,” Dagley went on, hurling his voice as though he wanted it to strike a blow. “You’ve no business coming here talking about sticks when you won’t give a stick to mend the place. Go and ask in Middlemarch what they think of _your_ character.”

“You’d do better to keep quiet, Dagley,” his wife said, “instead of kicking over your own trough. When a man with a family has spent money at market and drunk too much, he’s done enough harm for one day. But I’d like to know what my boy’s done, sir.”

“Never you mind what he’s done,” Dagley said more fiercely. “It’s my place to speak, not yours. And I will speak. I’ll have my say, supper or no supper. What I say is, I’ve lived on your land, and my father and grandfather before me, and we’ve sunk our money into it. Me and my children might lie down and rot there to manure the ground we can’t afford to buy manure for, if the King wasn’t going to stop it.”
“My good man, you’re drunk, you know,” Mr. Brooke said in a confidential, but unwise, tone. “Another day, another day,” he added, starting to turn away.

Dagley immediately stepped in front of him. Fag growled low at his master’s heels as the man’s voice rose in volume and insult; Monk moved close too, keeping a dignified, silent watch. The laborers on the wagon had stopped to listen. Standing still seemed wiser than an absurd attempt to flee with a shouting man in pursuit.

“I’m no drunker than you, and not so much,” said Dagley. “I can hold my drink, and I know what I mean. I mean the King will put a stop to it. People who know say there’s to be a Reform, and landlords who’ve never done right by their tenants will get such treatment they’ll have to run for it. There are people in Middlemarch who know what this Reform is, and know who’ll have to run. They say, ‘We know who _your_ landlord is.’ I say, ‘I hope knowing him does you more good than it does me.’ They say, ‘He’s a tight-fisted one.’ ‘That he is,’ I say. ‘He supports Reform,’ they say. That’s what they told me. And I found out what Reform meant: sending you and your sort running, with some pretty strong-smelling things after you too. Do what you like now; I’m not afraid of you. You’d better leave my boy alone and look to yourself before Reform gets on your back. That’s what I have to say.” Mr. Dagley ended by driving his fork so firmly into the ground that he had trouble pulling it out again.

At this gesture Monk began barking loudly, giving Mr. Brooke a chance to escape. He left the yard as quickly as possible, astonished by the unfamiliar situation. No one had ever insulted him on his own land before. He had tended to think himself liked by everyone, as we all do when we think more about our own amiability than about what others may need from us. When he quarreled with Caleb Garth twelve years earlier, he had supposed the tenants would welcome their landlord taking everything into his own hands.

Some readers following this account may marvel at the utter darkness of Mr. Dagley’s understanding. But in those days nothing was easier than for a farmer of his standing, working land his family had long held, to remain ignorant. Somehow this was possible despite a rector in the neighboring parish who was a gentleman through and through, a nearer curate whose sermons were more learned than the rector’s, a landlord who had looked into everything, especially art and social improvement, and all the enlightenment of Middlemarch only three miles away. To see how easily human beings evade knowledge, try an ordinary acquaintance amid London’s intellectual blaze. Consider what that desirable dinner guest might have become if his education had consisted of a little arithmetic from Tipton’s parish clerk, and he could scarcely struggle through a Bible chapter because names such as Isaiah and Apollos defeated him even after spelling them out twice. Poor Dagley sometimes read a few verses on Sunday evening, and at least the world grew no darker for him. Some things he knew thoroughly: the sloppy farming habits and the contrary ways of weather, livestock and crops at Freeman’s End. Apparently that name was sarcastic. A man was free to leave if he liked, but nowhere on earth beyond it was open to him.
